aiLab.title: AI Lab
aiLab.subtitle: Train real models on real data: a training set, a held-out test set and a shifted-condition test set. Every number comes from this run.
aiLab.empty: No experiments yet. Create one to start.

form.title: Experiment name
form.participationTip: Projected: the teacher operates, students predict and judge. Group: several students share one device. Individual: each student does every step. The mode decides which records count as personal evidence.

P1.title: Object or background?
P1.desc: Photograph 4 kinds of objects on the same background, then test on a new background to see what the model really learned.
P1.predictPrompt: If every photo is taken on the same desk, will the trained model still recognise the objects somewhere else? Write your prediction and your reason.

P2.title: Does it still work in a new setting?
P2.desc: Design your own table of test conditions, predict the accuracy, collect and verify each one, then add data and train a new version.
P2.predictPrompt: Which conditions will you change to challenge the model? Write the one most likely to break it, and why.

free.title: Free experiment
free.desc: Define your own classes, collect your own data and run the full train-and-test loop.
free.predictPrompt: Before you start: what should the model recognise, and where do you think it will fail?

L1.title: Can it tell my two things apart?
L1.desc: Pick two objects, take 10 photos of each, then test the model on held-out and shifted photos.
L1.predictPrompt: Which two objects did you pick? When do you think the AI will mix them up?

L3.title: What happens when AI is fed wrong data?
L3.desc: Train on clean data first, then deliberately mislabel 20% and train a second version to compare.
L3.predictPrompt: If 20% of the training photos get the wrong label, how much will the score drop? Write your guess.

L4.title: How many is enough?
L4.desc: Same data, train one version with 3, 10 and 30 photos per class and watch the accuracy.
L4.predictPrompt: 3, 10, 30 per class: will the score keep rising, or is there a point where more does not help?

M1.title: Campus detective: a full training run
M1.desc: Write a data card, collect 30 photos of six campus items each, then lock, train, test, improve and write a model card.
M1.predictPrompt: Which six items will you recognise? Which one will be hardest to photograph well, and why?

P3.title: Human rules vs data rules
P3.desc: On a table of data, write your own if-then rules first, then let a decision tree learn rules from the data and compare on the same test set.
P3.predictPrompt: Your rules or the rules the machine learns from data: which will be more accurate on unseen rows, and why?

P7.title: Can you trust AI-written campus news?
P7.desc: Split an AI-written campus article into claims, check each one against the original notice, then rewrite it into a trustworthy version.
P7.predictPrompt: The AI article reads smoothly. How many claims do you think disagree with the notice? Which kind of fact is most likely to be wrong?

L2.title: Can sounds be recognised too?
L2.desc: Record 10 clips each of clapping, knocking and whistling, then test with another student's sounds and classroom noise.
L2.predictPrompt: If a different student claps, will the AI still hear clapping? What about with classroom noise on top? Write your prediction.

P6.title: Campus sound map
P6.desc: Collect 15 clips of five campus sounds, test in new places and with noise, and build a sound map you can listen to.
P6.predictPrompt: Which five campus sounds will you record? Which two will the AI mix up most, and why?

M4.title: Keyword spotting: from sound to command
M4.desc: Record ten Chinese command words and test with other speakers and devices to see when voice commands break.
M4.predictPrompt: Will a model trained on your voice understand a classmate saying the same word? What about a recording from another phone?

M5.title: Emotion translator: text can be classified too
M5.desc: Two students label campus messages independently, measure agreement, train naive Bayes and test on a new topic.
M5.predictPrompt: Will two people give the same message the same emotion label? If the model learns canteen messages, will it still work on club messages?

M3.title: Decision tree vs neural network
M3.desc: Same table, same held-out set: train a tree and a small neural network and compare accuracy, explainability and shifted-set results.
M3.predictPrompt: A tree can be drawn; a neural network hides its rules. Which will be more accurate on unseen data?

L5.title: What is wrong in the AI's animal story?
L5.desc: The teacher projects an AI-written animal story; students find the hidden mistake using a field guide.
L5.predictPrompt: The AI's story sounds smooth. Do you think it could still be wrong somewhere?

L6.title: I make the rules
L6.desc: Write your own classification rules on animal or waste attribute cards, then compare with the rules the AI learns.
L6.predictPrompt: Which attribute will you use to split? Is one rule enough?

M2.title: Make the classifier fairer
M2.desc: Record who collected each photo, see how accuracy differs between collectors, then add data for the weaker group and retrain.
M2.predictPrompt: If most training photos come from one person, will the model be equally accurate on photos taken by others?

workspace.readOnlyHint: You are viewing someone else's experiment: data, metrics and the timeline are visible, nothing can be changed.

section.collectHint: Define the classes first, then photograph or upload for each class. At least {{min}} per class, and record the conditions.
section.lockHint: Locking randomly holds out {{pct}}% of each class as the test set. Training never sees them, so the score you get is trustworthy.
section.trainHint: Training runs inside your browser. Nothing is sent to an AI service.
section.testHint: The held-out set answers "did it learn?"; the shifted set answers "does it survive a new setting?". The difference is the generalisation gap.
section.shiftHint: New background, angle, light, device… collect and test them in the "shifted-condition" tab of the previous step.
section.shiftWhere: Shifted-condition sets are collected and run in the second tab of the held-out test card.
section.conditionHint: Write the condition and your predicted accuracy first, then collect and test. When the condition name matches a shifted set, the measured value fills in automatically.
section.errorsHint: Open the misclassified samples in the test results and use the heat map to see where the model is looking.
section.errorsWhere: Misclassified samples and heat maps are below the test results.
section.errorsMark: I have looked at the mistakes
section.iterateHint: Add data or adjust classes to fix what the tests exposed, train a new version and compare it side by side.
section.modelCardHint: In your own words: where this model can be used, where it cannot, and what the evidence is.
section.importHint: Import a training set and shifted sets from a preset pack; you can add your own photos too.
section.importTableHint: Import a preset table. Each row is one sample and its class.
section.importEmpty: This experiment uses preset data: import a pack first.
section.dataCardHint: Plan before collecting: the problem, the classes, where and how many to collect, and where it could be unfair.
section.mislabelHint: Train and test a clean version first; then let the system mislabel part of the training set and train another version to compare.
section.restoreHint: After comparing, restore the correct labels and train once more to confirm the score comes back.
section.rulesHint: Look at the table and the scatter plot, write if-then rules, try them on the training rows, then save them as a version.
section.treeHint: Let a decision tree find rules in the same training rows. Deeper trees make finer rules and memorise coincidences more easily.
section.shiftRowsHint: The shifted set is another batch of rows from a different source; test it on the second tab of the held-out test card.
section.errorsRowsHint: Expand the wrong rows in the test results to see which rule or branch decided them.
section.curveHint: Compare versions with different photos per class: does the score keep rising, or level off?
section.compareHint: Same held-out and shifted sets: how do your rules and the tree score, and on which class do they differ?
section.collectAudioHint: Define the classes, then record or upload for each. At least {{min}} one-second clips per class; note the speaker and place.
section.collectTextHint: At least {{min}} sentences per class. Import a preset corpus or add sentences yourself.
section.importAudioHint: Import a training set and shifted sets from a preset sound pack; add your own recordings if you have a microphone.
section.importTextHint: Import a preset corpus: one sentence and its emotion label per row.
section.audioTrainHint: Training runs in your browser: each clip becomes a spectrogram, then a pre-trained sound model extracts features.
section.textTrainHint: Naive Bayes counts how often each word appears in each class; after training you can see the 'emotion words' it learned.
section.mlpHint: Train a small neural network on the same training rows; watch the loss fall, then compare with the tree on the same test set.
section.annotateHint: Two students label the training sentences independently — no discussing yet.
section.agreementHint: Compute the agreement rate and kappa; discuss the disagreements and adopt one label.
section.fairnessHint: Below the held-out results, group accuracy by '{{tag}}' to find whom the model treats unfairly, then go back and collect more data for that group.
section.fairnessWhere: The per-group accuracy table is below the held-out test results.
section.shiftAudioHint: Another speaker, another place, added noise, another device… record and test on the second tab of the held-out test card.
section.shiftTextHint: The shifted set is messages on another topic; test it on the second tab of the held-out test card.
section.errorsAudioHint: Open the wrong clips in the test results, listen and look at the spectrogram, and think about why they were misheard.
section.compareMlpHint: Same held-out and shifted sets: how do the tree and the network score? Which is steadier, and which can explain itself?

shapes.title: Three shapes (synthetic)
shapes.desc: 40 circles, squares and triangles each: filled or hollow, random size, stroke and colour, wobbly edges and distractor dots. Shifted sets: dark background, patterned background, hand-drawn. Works without a camera.

campus-items.title: Campus items table (synthetic)
campus-items.desc: Size, weight and material of cups, pencil cases, books and basketballs; the shifted set comes from 'another school' with different sizes and materials.

penguins.title: Palmer penguins
penguins.desc: Bill, flipper, body mass, island and sex of three penguin species; 2007–2008 records for training, 2009 records as the shifted set.

iris.title: Iris flowers
iris.desc: Sepal and petal sizes of three iris species, 150 rows; write a rule like 'petal length under 2.5 means setosa' and compare with a tree.

sounds-synth.title: Four synthetic sounds
sounds-synth.desc: Whistles, knocks, claps and rustles, 30 clips each with varying pitch and rhythm; claps and knocks get confused with each other. Shifted sets: added classroom noise, different timbre, cheap microphone. Works without a microphone.

campus-messages.title: Campus message emotions
campus-messages.desc: 150 original campus messages labelled positive/negative/neutral; the shifted set switches to club-and-event topics.

animal-cards.title: Animal attribute cards
animal-cards.desc: 60 animal cards: legs, feathers, scales, habitat, flight, birth and more; the shifted set has exceptions like the platypus and the kiwi.

garbage-cards.title: Waste sorting cards
garbage-cards.desc: 60 item cards: material, recyclable, hazardous, rots, greasy → four waste classes.

flowers.title: Five flowers (photos)
flowers.desc: 50 real photos each of sunflowers, roses, daisies, dandelions and tulips; within a class the size, angle and background all vary, so the held-out set produces real mistakes. Shifted sets: blurred, dark, zoomed-in.

fruits-varied.title: Six fruits (mixed varieties)
fruits-varied.desc: Apples, bananas, cherries, grapes, oranges and peaches from Fruits-360, each class mixing several varieties; the 'new variety' set holds varieties never seen in training, the background sets paste the same fruit onto colourful and dark backgrounds.

mislabel.restoreIntro: Restore every changed label, then train once more to confirm the score comes back.
